Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

We have reserved the North Hall auditorium, which has 84 seats, but the reservation is not a statement that we expect to fill it. The room is also used by the debate team, so our equipment and boxes need to be cleared out after each event.

The program is about interiors and the ways people use them, rather than being a strict historical survey. The first night is planned around two short films from the regional archive, and the next three evenings each have one feature-length film under consideration. We have not yet received the archive’s written confirmation for the second feature. It is in the same broad theme, but it has a quieter pace than the rest, which may make the transition between films a little uneven if we keep the short pair on night one. I think that is manageable, although I would not describe it as a completely settled running order.

Maya Chen is coordinating the archive messages, and she said, “They told me the rights form is in the review queue, not that it has been approved.” That wording matters because volunteers have already asked whether they can put the title on the printed card. We are holding the card design until the society has permission in writing. If written rights confirmation for the second feature has not arrived by August 18, we will replace it with the already licensed short program that Ravi has proposed. This is a contingency, not a decision that the feature has been rejected, and the program note should not describe it as one.

The other three titles are still being compared for fit and cost. The first feature is available through the campus library, but its delivery link expires on October 6, so someone will need to test it before the final screening date and not assume that a link which works in September will keep working. The third title is offered by a small distributor at a student rate, with a separate caption file. We have asked whether the captions are included in that rate, and the reply has not arrived. The fourth evening might use a locally made documentary if the group can confirm that the filmmaker is comfortable with a public campus screening; at present, we only have an informal conversation about that possibility.

There are several practical items beyond choosing the films. Joel will ask facilities to unlock the auditorium at 5:30 p.m. each evening, while the first screening is listed to begin at 6:15. The volunteers need time to check the projector, set out the captioning receiver, and place the program cards near the entrance. The projector sometimes makes skin tones look slightly warm, according to Maya, but she has not tested it with these files yet. We should do a test with a sample file before the first event rather than treating her observation as a confirmed problem with the selected films.

1. Publicity and printed material: Nia is drafting a one-page schedule for the campus noticeboards and a shorter announcement for the society mailing list. The noticeboard version needs the dates, room, start time, and the series title; it should not promise that a particular title will appear until the rights and screening permissions are settled. We usually get more questions about captions than about the film descriptions, so the announcement can mention that caption access is being checked without saying that every file is confirmed. The mailing list will go out after the printed card is approved.

2. Access and seating: The auditorium has a step-free entrance from the east corridor, and four seats can be removed from the front row if wheelchair spaces are needed. The society has not received any seating requests so far. Priya will check the receiver batteries and place a brief instruction card beside the sign-in sheet. She says people occasionally miss the receiver table when it is set too close to the doorway, so it may be better to put it beside the welcome desk. That is a suggestion for the room layout, not a confirmed accommodation request from a guest.

3. Volunteer roles: For each screening, two volunteers will stay near the door, one will manage the projector, and one will keep track of attendance. The remaining people can rotate between greeting guests and restocking the water jug. We do not charge admission, but the society plans to put out a voluntary contribution jar for future license costs. The jar is not connected to entry, and the announcement should make that clear if it mentions contributions. The club has not set a fundraising target for this series.

4. Follow-up and review: After October 3, the committee intends to collect short comments from attendees and review which practical arrangements worked. Ravi suggested a paper slip as well as a QR code because some visitors do not want to use a phone during an event. We have not chosen the questions yet, and no one is being asked to submit a name. The review is meant to help with the next program, not to rank the films or claim that one screening was more successful than another. If the archive confirmation misses the August 18 date, the schedule and the review sheet will both need the replacement program name before they are printed.

The society is keeping the series modest because volunteers also have coursework and other club events during September. We can probably staff the current plan, but the availability sheet has two unanswered entries for October 3, so the committee should not treat that evening’s assignments as complete. The film descriptions can stay brief, with one sentence about each film’s use of space and a note about its source. The final room checklist should include the auditorium key, the projector test, the receiver, the sign-in sheet, and removal of the society’s materials afterward.
